titleStmt.title: Paper Prepared in the National Security Council

div.head: Paper Prepared in the National Security Council
div.p: The US recently proposed to grandfather the downloading of both the SS–N–18 and the Minuteman III missiles, but to ban further downloading (see attached talking points). The Soviets rejected this US proposal. In preparation for the upcoming Bartholomew-Obukov meetings in Geneva, the US should review its downloading position.

The US initially proposed downloading primarily to permit the deployment of MM IIIs with one RV, thereby allowing the US to retain a larger silo-based ICBM force in START I. The right to download SLBMs also is of interest in the context of a hedge against a possible 3000–4000 accountable warhead START II limit.
The USAF currently plans to download Minuteman III missiles by 1 or 2 warheads each on 300 missiles at two bases. A right to download an aggregate of 600 RVs would protect this Minuteman option.

The Navy would require an aggregate of at least 864 RVs to protect future SLBM downloading requirements, assuming that downloading provisions would allow the downloading of the current two types of missiles on the Trident submarines or that the D–5 would be backfitted to all submarines.
Taken together, these MM III and SLBM options would require the right to download 2 RVs from each of 2 or 3 types of missiles, within an aggregate limit of about 1500 downloaded RVs.

The Soviets, after an initial resistance to downloading, announced that the SS–N–18 should now count at 3 RVs instead of 7 RVs per missile (a difference of 896 RVs), and propose to allow downloading of an aggregate of 1250 warheads on 2 additional types of missiles.

In order to use this large aggregate limit effectively, the Soviets would probably seek to download their SS–N–20 and SS–24 missiles by at least 5 RVs each. A right to download an aggregate of 1060 RVs (in addition to the SS–N–18) would probably be required to satisfy Soviet
objectives. If the SS–N–18 is treated as a downloaded missile, the Soviet approach amounts to the right to download up to 5 RVs from each of three types of missiles, within an aggregate limit of about 2000 RVs.

There are three variables that could be used to define downloading options: (1) the number of types of missiles that could be downloaded; (2) the number of RVs that could be downloaded from each missile; and, (3) the aggregate number of RVs that could be downloaded.

Each of the following options assumes that the SS–N–18 would be captured as a downloaded missile, that base-by-base downloading would be allowed, that downloading of heavy ICBMs would be banned, and that there would be one extra RV inspection per year per base where downloaded missiles are deployed.

list.label: A.
list.item:
Grandfather SS–N–18 and MM III RV attribution (current US position). –
Download 4 RVs per missile for SS–N–18. –
Download 2 RV per missile for MM III. –
No aggregate limit.

list.label: B.
list.item:
Download an aggregate of 1000 RVs for each side on existing types of missiles. –
Either ICBMs or SLBMs. –
No limit on the number of different types of missiles. –
As types of downloaded missiles are retired, additional existing types may be downloaded.

list.label: C.
list.item:
Grandfather the SS–N–18 and MM III attribution separate from downloading. Download up to two RVs per missile on one additional type of existing missile with an aggregate limit of 500 RVs. –
Either ICBMs or SLBMs.

list.label: D.
list.item:
Download up to two RVs per missile on three existing types of missiles. –
Except the SS–N–18 could be downloaded by four RVs per missile. –
Either ICBMs or SLBMs –
No aggregate limit.
